title: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
hook: a companion whose recitation the Prophet ﷺ likened to the pipes of the family of Dawud

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ansar women who asked the Prophet for a day of their own. Your line was: a day for learning. Did the person you'll teach get a date? Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

Night in Medina. A man is reciting the Qur'an, for no one in particular. He doesn't know that out in the dark, someone has stopped to listen. The next day the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells him: if only you had seen me last night, listening to your recitation. Then he adds a compliment. You have been given one of the pipes of the family of Dawud. Today: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, a man from Yemen with a voice worth stopping for.
screen: `RECITING AT NIGHT, ALONE.` → `SOMEONE STOPS TO LISTEN.` → `A PIPE OF DAWUD'S FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Start with the compliment. The word in the hadith is mizmar, a reed pipe, a wind instrument. Dawud, the prophet David, is remembered in the Qur'an as one with whom the mountains and the birds joined in praise. So when the Prophet said Abu Musa had a pipe of Dawud's family, he was saying: your voice carries something of that. Muslim and Bukhari both record it. But here's the turn. Abu Musa is also the companion who narrates a very different kind of lesson about voices. On a journey, he reports, the companions were climbing and calling out God is greatest at the top of their lungs. And the Prophet told them to go easy on themselves. You are not calling on someone deaf or absent, he said. You are calling on One who hears, and who is near. Put those two reports side by side. The sweet voice was heard at night, unplanned, not on a stage. And the loud voices were gently quieted. Beauty in recitation, in these reports, is not about volume. It's about a sense that the One addressed is close. There's a third picture of Abu Musa's people that fits. Bukhari records the Prophet praising the Ash'aris, Abu Musa's tribe, because when their food ran low they gathered everything they had on one cloth and shared it out equally. They are from me, he said, and I am from them. A people known for sharing, and one of them known for a voice. Neither the food nor the voice was kept to themselves.
screen: `MIZMAR, A REED PIPE.` · `NOT DEAF, NOT ABSENT: NEAR.` · `BEAUTY IS CARE, NOT VOLUME.` · `THE ASH'ARIS SHARED THEIR FOOD.` · then, large: `A VOICE LIKE DAWUD'S.`

segments.voice: The practice: recite softly and well. Let the room go quiet around you. If you know a short surah, or even al-Fatiha, you can say it now, quietly, almost under your breath. Slowly. Give each letter its place. Don't rush the long vowels. If you don't recite, you can do the same with any words that matter to you, or simply listen to your own breathing as if it were a sound worth tending. Not loud. Close. As if speaking to someone who is near. The bell holds the time.
Abu Musa. A companion from Yemen whose recitation the Prophet compared to a pipe of the family of Dawud, and who also reported: you call on One who hears, and is near. Today's word.
Your line: a voice like Dawud's. Today, the next time you feel the urge to raise your voice to be heard, lower it instead, once. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims value beautiful, careful recitation of the Qur'an (tajwid), and Abu Musa's reported gift comes up when people speak of reciting with a lovely voice.

fork.reveal: Abu Musa reports he told them to go easy on themselves: you are not calling on one deaf or absent, but One who hears, and is near.

original.note: Arabic: a reed pipe, the word in the hadith about Abu Musa's voice.

trapdoor: what you thought: a companion famous for a loud, powerful voice.
what it means: the Prophet heard him reciting quietly at night and likened his voice to a pipe of the family of Dawud.
what a scholar hears: mizmar, a reed pipe, set beside Abu Musa's other report that God is near and hears, so there is no need to shout.

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory: confirm Muslim 793, Bukhari 5048, 2992, 2486.
The 'night' and 'in his own home' framing follows Muslim 793 ('if you had seen me while I listened to your recitation last night'); confirm the setting is not overstated.
Year 1 (day 229) and year 2 (day 543) already mention the mizmar hadith; today's angle adds the 'not deaf or absent' report and the Ash'aris' sharing. Confirm acceptable.
